clue.text: Plant, gaudy, with unpleasant smell

parts.note: a vine is a climbing plant
gaudy means garish, showy and bright

explanation.surface: A garden plant is described as both flashy in colour and foul-smelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that reeks sourly, like soured wine, can be called smelly in that sharp acidic way.

clue.text: This shows views of the electorate from the start

definitions.text: This shows views of the electorate from the start

indicators.note: from the start picks the opening letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: This reveals what the voting public thinks, right from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters of 'views of the electorate' spell the answer, and the whole clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot is how the electorate expresses its views, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Warnings received by amphibian in Hampshire area

indicators.note: received by says the warnings go inside the amphibian

parts.note: a newt is a small amphibian
fore is the golfer's shouted warning, so warnings are fores

explanation.surface: A newt in Hampshire is alerted by a series of warnings.
explanation.walkthrough: THE NEW FOREST is a national park in Hampshire, a county in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an ancient woodland and heath district in the English county of Hampshire, so a named area there.

clue.text: What you do with torticollis — suffer severely

definitions.meaning: torticollis is a painful twisted neck, so literally you have pain in that part
be punished or hit hard, take the brunt

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be harshly punished, and literally describes having a painful neck condition.

clue.text: Harsh treatment, given untreated wood

parts.note: raw means unprocessed, untreated
deal is pine or fir timber

explanation.surface: Someone is handed rough timber, a harsh way to be treated.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAL is a crossword favourite for softwood timber. 'given' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting unfair or harsh treatment is idiomatically called getting a bad deal.

clue.text: Bad as it can get right out of order

indicators.note: out of order means jumbled, so these letters are put in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Things are as bad as can be, completely unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right out of order' sounds like British slang for unacceptable, but it rearranges AS IT CAN. 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means devilish, so evil, a strong sense of bad.

clue.text: A member of parliament attached to Conservative party

explanation.surface: An MP joins up with the Conservative Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attached to' is only a joining phrase here; the pieces simply sit side by side, C then A then MP.
explanation.definitionFit: A camp is a faction or group holding a shared view, a sense close to a political party.

clue.text: A party put to shame

parts.note: a bash is an informal party

explanation.surface: Someone at a party is embarrassed.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash is to make someone embarrassed or ashamed, the same as to shame them.

clue.text: Train speed varies — that's commonplace

indicators.note: varies suggests the letters change into a different order

explanation.surface: A train's speed keeps changing, which is quite ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian as an adjective means dull and ordinary, just like commonplace.

clue.text: In fine fettle, working a la distaff side

indicators.note: working means the letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone in great shape is busy on the female side of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The distaff side is the female line of a family.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in fine fettle is to be in excellent health, the meaning of the idiom.

clue.text: In other words, something that owl might produce

definitions.meaning: a formal phrase introducing a restatement, meaning namely
the first half of the traditional hoot attributed to the tawny owl, spelt this way

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means namely, and it also sounds like the owl's call of to-whit to-whoo.

clue.text: Weather that's awful in gale

indicators.note: in says the scrambled letters sit inside the word for gale

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

indicators.note: awful suggests the letters of the word are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Some awful weather arrives in the form of a gale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weather' is the verb, to survive or come through, not the climate; 'awful' makes THSTA, and 'in' sets it inside the gale word.
explanation.definitionFit: To weather a storm is to endure or resist it, a verb sense matching the answer.

clue.text: Throngs milling around those responsible for rescues — they're phenomenal

indicators.note: around says the scrambled crowd surrounds the rescuers' letters
milling crowds move about confusedly, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the scrambled letters
THE RNLI, the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, the British charity that runs the lifeboats

explanation.surface: Crowds mill around the lifeboat rescuers, who are doing a fantastic job.
explanation.walkthrough: The RNLI is Britain's volunteer lifeboat service. 'Phenomenal' is meant literally: the aurora is a natural phenomenon, not merely amazing.
explanation.definitionFit: The aurora borealis is a natural light display, literally a set of phenomena in the sky.

clue.text: Intense disappointment produced by card on holiday

parts.note: a heart is a playing card of that suit
a break is a short holiday

explanation.surface: A postcard sent on holiday brings great disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbreak is overwhelming sorrow or grief, a strong form of disappointment.

clue.text: Road round steep turn appearing endless

indicators.note: turn tells us the whole assembled piece is read backwards
round says the road word goes about the soaking word

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road
to ret is to steep flax or hemp in water

explanation.surface: A road winds round a steep bend that seems to go on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steep' is the verb, to soak flax, not an adjective. 'round' gives LANRETE, and 'turn' reverses all of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal things have no end, so it is a direct synonym of endless.

clue.text: Firework —- a fine example

definitions.meaning: a small explosive party novelty or banger
informal praise for something excellent, a corker

explanation.definitionFit: It is both a bang-snap firework and slang for an outstanding specimen of something.

clue.text: Anchor containing two metals -that makes for a dangerous situation

indicators.note: containing says the anchor goes round the metals

parts.note: a kedge is a small anchor
Ni is the chemical symbol for nickel
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: An anchor made of two metals makes a perilous spot for sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: The two metals are nickel and iron; 'containing' sets them inside the small anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a knife-edge means being in a precarious position, one where things could go either way.

clue.text: Gags voiced by swine

indicators.note: voiced tells us to go by how the word is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: swine as an insult means contemptible people, wretches

explanation.surface: Someone is choked off by a gang of swine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gags' is the verb, heaves as if to vomit, not jokes or muzzles.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag is to heave involuntarily in the throat, the same as to retch.

clue.text: Arrangement relating to attack

parts.note: a setup is an arrangement
on means about, relating to

explanation.surface: An arrangement relating to an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: To be set upon is to be attacked, so the phrasal verb means assault.

clue.text: Dropping back, short of energy, revitalises, showing fortitude

indicators.note: dropping back indicates the remaining letters are read in reverse
short of says a letter is missing from the word

parts.note: to animate is to bring to life, revitalise
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A runner drops back, low on energy, then recovers and shows grit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short of energy' removes E from ANIMATES to leave ANIMATS, and 'Dropping back' reverses that. 'showing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is staying power, the endurance that goes with fortitude.

clue.text: Sprinkle the salt around in secrecy

indicators.note: sprinkle suggests scattering, so the letters are mixed up
around supports the scattering instruction, letters strewn about

explanation.surface: Secretly sprinkling salt around.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealth means acting covertly, the same as secrecy.

clue.text: Old-fashioned reader of paper may be invisible thus

definitions.meaning: out of date, not keeping up

definitions.text: reader of paper may be invisible thus
definitions.meaning: someone reading a broadsheet is hidden at the rear of the open newspaper of that name

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means out of date, and literally describes someone hidden behind a copy of the London paper.

clue.text: Jack, one enlisted in army

indicators.note: enlisted in says the numeral goes inside the army

parts.note: host is an old word for an army
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A sailor named Jack is one who joined the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name or sailor; it is the verb, to lift with a jack.
explanation.definitionFit: To jack something up is to lift it, as one would hoist it.

clue.text: Some fancy stitches employed in pouch

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Decorative stitching used on a little bag.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'employed in pouch' as the definition, but the answer means just 'pouch'; 'employed in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyst is a sac or bladder in the body, a pouch-like structure.

clue.text: Prelate's poem about saint — a gem!

indicators.note: about says the poem goes round the saint

parts.note: an epic is a long narrative poem
an opal is a gemstone

explanation.surface: A bishop's verse about a saint is called a real jewel.
explanation.definitionFit: Episcopal means relating to bishops, so it works as the adjective for a prelate's.

clue.text: Pop? Popped one's clogs twice in twenty-four hours

indicators.note: in places the two letters inside the word for a day

parts.note: a day lasts twenty-four hours

indicators.note: twice asks for the died letter to be used two times

parts.note: D stands for died, as in genealogies; popping one's clogs is British slang for dying

explanation.surface: A father died twice in a single day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popped one's clogs' is British slang for died, abbreviated D as in family trees. 'twice' doubles it and 'in' puts DD inside DAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is an informal name for a father, as is daddy.

clue.text: Tackle enemy's first plane

parts.note: tackle means gear or equipment, kit

indicators.note: first takes just the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Taking on the enemy's leading aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tackle' looks like a verb, to engage, but it is the noun meaning gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A kite was RAF slang for an aeroplane, and is also a light tethered flying frame.

clue.text: Coin the English pocketed, as it turned out

indicators.note: pocketed says the other letters go inside the coining word

parts.note: to coin a word is to invent it
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Englishman slips a coin into his pocket, as things turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coin' is a verb, to make up, not money; 'pocketed' sets the other letters inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in the end, as things happened, the same as as it turned out.
